title: Chapter 127 – Leave of Absence
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The Dock keeps a list of its sisters, and has never shown it to him.

He finds it on a gray morning in the first month of the new year, in the cold green hush of the Gate stair, when he is no longer looking for it. The Cole door has been open in his soul for half a year. He has learned its habits: the faint pressure at the breastbone, the quiet hum like a held note, the way it brightens when he thinks about the sky. He has learned that when he stops straining, it speaks.

He stands in front of the Gate wall, with his palm on Qin Hao's old hand-print, and thinks of nothing. And a panel opens in his sight, plain and square, without being summoned.

```
DOCK REGISTER — ARK-3 (Azure Cloud site)
Tier: 2 (Reservoir installed)
Seated: Fragment 1 [LOCK] Fragment 2 [KEY]
Unseated: Fragment 3 [DOOR]
Sister sites on record:
ARK-1 status: DARK bearing: unknown
ARK-2 status: DARK bearing: unknown
ARK-4 status: DARK bearing: WEST, ~3,400 li
ARK-5 status: DARK bearing: SOUTH, ~1,900 li
ARK-6 status: [no record]
ARK-7 status: [this interface]
Note: sister-site logs are readable ONLY from the site.
Note: bench synthesis is not portable.
```

He reads it three times. Then, because he is a careful man, he reads it a fourth.

Readable only from the site.

It is the answer he has been circling for six months and refusing to hear. The first Operator's note had said, ask where the Operators went. The Chain had said, the eighth. Neither had told him how to find the other seven. This does: seven sites, five of them with a bearing or a name, and every one of them dark. Dark, not dead. Dark as a lamp is dark in an empty room.

He takes his hand off the wall. The panel does not close.

```
Field draw: LABOR ONLY while off-site.
Reservoir: LOCKED to ARK-3 (15 / 200). Will not travel.
Door in Autumn: 2 CE per reading. Seam Needle: ~6 CE.
Carry cell: 12 CE maximum.
```

Will not travel.

That is the price. It is not a thing he can bargain with; it is the cost of the road. If he walks away from the stair, he leaves behind the bench that lets him print a pill from a sheet of paper and a pinch of dust. He leaves behind the Spring Vein, the winter bank, the fifteen CE it took him two seasons to earn back. He takes twelve units of strength in a pouch at his belt, and whatever he can scrape from honest labor, two a night, six a week. A man with twelve can make a Needle. A man with twelve cannot make a Golden Core.

He stands in the green light a long while.

Then he says, aloud, to the empty stair, "All right."

* * *

The Sect Council takes up his request on the fourth day of the month, in the Hall of Elders, in a room that has changed.

It is a smaller room than he remembers, or perhaps he has grown. The long table is the same black lacquer. The walls still bear the faded murals of the Founders ascending a mountain, nine robed figures with their arms raised, and a tenth lagging behind. But the nine chairs along the table no longer all face the head. Some have been turned a little, toward each other, as if their occupants had begun, at last, to listen.

Wuping presides, in the Cloud Peak seat. He is a lean, sallow, intelligent man of sixty, with careful hands, and he has held the post for six months. He has not yet decided whether he likes it. Beside him sits the new Law Elder, a woman called Shu, who replaced Mu and has not yet said a word that was not a question. Across from them, Treasury, Pill Hall, Sutra. In the corner chair sits Qin Hao, Elder Emeritus, with his stone hands resting on his knees like two grave-markers.

And in a new chair, a little apart, a small woman in a plain gray robe with a thick black ledger on her lap: Lin Yue, Head of the Seat of the Garden.

"Gate Bearer," says Wuping. "You have asked leave."

"I have."

"For how long?"

"I do not know."

A faint rustle. Shu's pen stops.

"I will not insult the Council with a number I cannot keep," Jian says. He stands in the middle of the floor, in his plain gray cloak, with his hands clasped in front of him, and he speaks without hurry. "There are places, some distance from here, that I have reason to believe hold the answer to a question that has cost this Sect a great deal. The Offering. The Registry. The Chain on the ridge. Perhaps the Gate itself. I think the answer is not in this valley. I think it is in the south and the west, in rooms I have not seen. I cannot say how long it will take to find them. Years, I suspect. More than a few."

"Years," repeats the Treasury Elder, a plump, anxious man named Lu. "And the Gate? You are the Bearer. The Gate is yours."

"The Gate is the Sect's. The stair is the Seat's to hold. It does not need me to stand in front of it." He turns his head. "Elder Qin Hao has held it before."

"With his body," says Qin Hao, from the corner. His voice is calm. "I would do it again."

"That is what I am afraid of."

The old man smiles, very slightly. "Boy. I am eighty-nine. I have outlived two Heads and three Treasurers. I did not expect to do any of it. Let me have the stair."

Wuping rubs the bridge of his nose. "And the Registry? You are leaving us exposed to the one organization on this mountain that has already killed our Law Elder."

"The Registry has withdrawn. It has asked for a name from the Seat. It has not asked for mine."

"Yet."

"Yet." Jian inclines his head. "That is a fair word. I cannot promise that it will stay quiet. I can only say that it has taken a great deal of effort to keep it quiet this long, and that my presence is not what has done it. Qin Hao's wall did that. The Seat's doors did that. They will go on doing it whether I am here or not."

Silence. At the back of the room Yue lifts her pen.

"May the Seat speak?"

"The Seat has a voice," says Wuping, with a faint sigh. "Speak."

* * *

She speaks for four minutes, and does not once look at her notes.

She says that the Seat of the Garden regards the Gate Bearer's leave as a service to the Sect, not a withdrawal from it. She says the Seat will pay the cost of his charter from its own grain, and the cost of his protection from its own staff, and the cost of his return from its own prayers. She says that the Seat will keep the Gate Stair's tally with the help of Elder Qin Hao, and report it each quarter to the Council. She says that Lin Jian is not the Seat's property, that he does not belong to the Garden, and that he has never asked it to hold him; but that the Seat would regard it as a personal insult if the Council tried to.

Nobody moves.

"A charter," says Yue, folding her hands. "Twelve years. Renewable by the vote of the Seat. A Gate Bearer on lawful travel, under the protection of the Sect, with all privileges of his rank. If the Council wishes to add conditions, the Seat will consider them." She pauses. "It would like to point out, however, that it has been asked for a great deal since the Offering and has given every time. Perhaps this once the Council might give."

The Treasury Elder is staring at her. Shu, the new Law Elder, has written something at the top of her page and underlined it twice.

"It is irregular," Wuping says finally.

"Yes," says Yue.

"It is also, I think, correct." He glances down the table. "Does the Council object?"

Nobody does.

"Then it is granted." He signs. The stamp thumps. "Twelve years, Gate Bearer, with the Seat's right to renew. Return when you can." A pause, and then, more quietly, the tired voice of a man who has been given a chair he never wanted: "And if you find an answer, tell us. I would like very much to be told."

Jian bows.

Qin Hao, in the corner, lifts one stone hand an inch from his knee and lets it fall. It is the closest thing to applause that he can manage.

* * *

Qinghe has been packing since before dawn.

It is a thing he should have expected. He comes into the back room at dusk and finds her kneeling on the floor in her stocking feet, with a blue cloth spread in front of her and a mountain of small folded things on it. Socks, wool. Two spare short robes. A needle case. A bundle of silver-thread, as if he would need it. Four jars of salve. A tin of dried plums. Three pairs of leggings, patched. A small wooden spoon. A candle.

"Mother."

"I know." She does not look up. "It is too much. I have been told. Your father came in at noon and said, Qinghe, he is not walking to the end of the world, and I said, Then he will not need to carry it far." She folds a shirt in thirds and sets it on the pile. "I am old. I am entitled."

"I will not have room."

"You will make room." She picks up the spoon and turns it over in her hands. It is plain, pale, smooth with age. "Do you remember this?"

He does not. He looks at it for a long time, trying, and the blank space behind his breastbone hums faintly.

"It was yours," says Qinghe, very gently. "When you were small. You would eat nothing else. You threw the others on the floor." She smiles. "Your father carved it. He said it was too much trouble to wait for you to grow into a proper one."

"I do not remember it."

"No. I know." She holds it out. "I do."

He takes it. The wood is warm from her hands, and for a moment, in the dim room, in the smell of dried plums and old cloth, he almost thinks that something moves, deep down, the shape of a small round face and a spoon and a lamp. Then it is gone, like a fish turning in a pond.

"There," says his mother. "You have it now. Whenever it goes, you hold it. It remembers for you."

"I cannot carry everything the family remembers."

"No. Only the spoon." She wipes her eyes with her wrist, impatiently. "I am not crying. It is the dust."

"I did not say anything."

"Good." She returns to her folding. "I told Bai I would go second. I told you. I meant it. But I am a stubborn old woman and I will not be dying while you are on the road." Her voice is steady. "You will go, and find what you need, and come back. When you come back, I will be at the gate with a pot of rice. I will be sixty-five and grumbling. You will bring me a pill, and I will take it, and I will outlive both of you out of spite."

"Mother—"

"That is my wish." She looks at him then, directly, with her small shrewd eyes. "Do not take it from me."

He kneels beside her on the floor, and puts his arms around her. She is very small. She smells of mint and smoke. She holds him with a strength that has no business in a body that age, and says nothing, and he understands that all the words in the room have been used up.

* * *

Yue is waiting for him on the stair.

She is in travel clothes, a short gray robe, belted, with a pack across her shoulders. She sits on the third step with her ledger in her lap, and Pebble beside her in the lamplight, and a small satchel at her feet. She does not look like a woman at the head of a Seat. She looks like a girl about to run away from home.

"No," says Jian.

"I have not said anything."

"You are dressed to travel."

"I am dressed for the weather." Her voice is perfectly mild. "He said to bring someone who hears seams. I am someone who hears seams. Pebble is the other, but Pebble cannot read a Dock register. She can only tell me what it sounds like."

"The Seat needs its head."

"The Seat has three heads. Father holds the door in the day. Feng holds it at night. Mother holds it in between." She does not smile. "I have written the schedule. It is in the ledger. I have left a copy under the pillow of each, so that none of them can claim they did not see it."

"It is a year's journey. At least."

"I will go as far as the first Dock," says Yue. "That is what I told them. Six months, perhaps eight. I will come back with the Tan caravan when the road is safe. Then you go on." She meets his eyes. "You need me for the first, Jian. You do not know what it is going to sound like. I do."

He stares at her. Pebble looks up, ears forward, as if hoping.

"What did Father say?"

"That he would rather lose a hand than let me go." A faint, rueful smile. "And that he would rather lose both than make me stay. Mother said nothing. She packed a second spoon."

He lets out a long breath. He has argued with the Council, with the Chain, with the House, with a thousand years of unkind rules. He has never won an argument with his sister.

"The first Dock," he says. "Not one step farther."

"Not one."

"And if it is bad—"

"I will stay behind you." She says it like a promise. "But I will not stay at home."

* * *

Bai gives him his parting gift at the door of the Pill Hall, in the rain.

It is a light cold rain, the first of the thaw, and the old man stands in the shelter of the eaves with a small oilcloth bundle held out in both trembling hands, and a look on his face of great, irritable tenderness. Behind him the furnaces glow. The smell of bitter herbs rolls out into the wet.

"Take it."

"What is it?"

"Eleven pills. Level two, high grade, three kinds. The red ones for blood loss, the white for fever, the green for when you have been foolish enough to eat something you found." He pushes the bundle into Jian's chest. "And a letter. Do not read it until you are at least a hundred li away."

"Master Bai."

"I am not your master. I told you that." But the old man's mouth twitches. "I told Qinghe I would make her a Foundation pill when the time comes, and I will. I told your father the same, and I did. I told that stubborn girl in the Sutra Hall I would keep her alive until she finishes reading, and I mean to. I have a great many promises and I intend to outlive every one." He glares up at the sky. "So you will not keep me waiting."

"I will not."

"Good." The old man hesitates. His eyes behind the thick lenses are not quite steady. "The ninth. I will send the root every season. I have already set a boy to it. If it fails, I will tell you."

"How?"

"How do I tell a man on the road?" Bai snorts. "Pebble will hear it. She hears everything. Ask the beast." He turns away, stiffly, and stops in the doorway with his back to Jian. "Boy."

"Yes?"

"You were the worst apprentice I ever had. You asked too many questions, you never did anything the proper way, and you cured a man I had given up on." The thin voice cracks. "I would not trade you for the finest pupil in the three Courts."

He goes in, and shuts the door. Jian stands in the rain with the bundle in his hands and does not move for a long time.

* * *

On the last night, he walks to the Sutra Hall to say goodbye to Ye, and finds her sitting on the floor of the stacks with a scroll across her knees.

She does not rise. She is a hundred and one, and her knees have been telling her so for a week. She sits in a pool of lamplight in the long dim aisles, between the shelves, with the black stick across her lap and the scroll of plum-colored paper unrolled to its first fold, and in front of her, on a low stool, sits a man in the gray of a Registry clerk.

He is perhaps forty. He is crying without a sound.

Jian stops in the doorway. He does not breathe.

"Say it again," says Ye, quietly, in the oldest script.

"I cannot." The man is shaking. "I cannot hear it. It is gone. It was there and now it is gone, I had it a moment ago—"

"You did not lose it. It was taken. Listen." Ye puts a finger on the scroll. Her voice is soft, patient, a schoolteacher's voice. "Pei Wanli."

The man flinches as if struck.

"Pei Wanli," says Ye again. "Who sang while he worked. Who was born the second of the third month, in a village called Lower Weir, to a fisherman named Pei Gen. Who burned his name at twenty-four to feed his sister's debts. Who has served the House for sixteen years. Who has a scar on his left thumb, from a net." She lifts her eyes. "Pei Wanli. You are home."

The man makes a sound that has nothing human in it.

He falls forward, onto his knees, onto his hands, and Ye reaches out and catches his shoulder with her old spotted fingers and holds him there, while he weeps like a child in the dust of the Sutra Hall. And from somewhere deep in his chest, thin and cracked and shaking, rises a song. A fisherman's work song. Four lines. He sings it through twice, and breaks off, and begins again.

"There," says Ye.

She looks up. She has seen him in the doorway; she has known all along. Her face is wet and utterly steady.

"It works," she says. "He is the first. There are four thousand more."

"I thought it might."

"You thought nothing of the kind. You thought I would fail." She is almost smiling. "I did not tell you in order to be thanked. I told you in order that you would know, when you stand in some cold room in the south, that there are people behind you doing the work that cannot be done by a man who is leaving."

He bows to her, as low as he has ever bowed to anyone.

"Go," says Ye. "I will read until I die. Come back and tell me what you found, and I will tell you who is left."

* * *

They leave at the third watch, by the north postern, in the dark.

Qin Hao is waiting at the Gate stair's head. He does not speak. He steps aside from the wall and lets Jian pass, and as Jian goes by, he lifts one stone hand a little, clumsily, and presses something into his palm with the flat of his fingers. It is a small thing, warm, round and heavy. A Gate warden's token, bronze, worn smooth by decades of thumbs.

"It was mine," he says. "From the day I first took the stair. It does not open anything. It only tells the wall that you are a friend."

"Elder."

"Keep it." The big gray face is very still. "In case you forget which side of the door you were born on."

Kuang walks them to the foot of the mountain, in his Inner Sect sash, and does not trust himself to say more than three words. Jian does not make him. At the last turn of the road, where the pines give way to open scrub and the first gray of dawn is breaking over the plain, Kuang stops, and bows, and says only, "Come back whole."

"I will try."

"Try harder."

Then they are on the road, the three of them, and the Garden is a smudge of smoke on the ridge behind. Pebble trots at Yue's heel. Yue walks with her pack straight and her chin up and her eyes on the horizon. Jian carries his mother's spoon in his breast pocket, wrapped in a handkerchief, against his heart.

It is a good road. It is wide and gray and dry, and the sun climbs, and the south wind brings the smell of ripening fields. They meet the Tan caravan at noon, seven wagons and thirty guards at a crossroads, with Ruyan's cousin at the head, a plump, polite man who offers them tea. They ride in the third wagon, among sacks of lacquer and bolts of cloth, and Yue falls asleep against a barrel with her ledger on her chest.

Ruyan's cousin, whose name is Tan Bo, pours the tea himself, with a flourish, and explains in a low voice that the caravan carries sixty-one tons of lacquer and silk and eleven passengers who have paid to be forgotten. The southern road, he says, is longer than it looks and shorter than it feels, and the only rule on it is that nobody asks where anybody is going. Yue listens with her head tilted. Jian drinks, and nods, and does not say that he has no idea.

For the first time in his life, Jian is alone with nothing to do.

He sits in the sway of the wagon and watches the fields go by. He thinks about the Dock. About the Chain. About a ninth sleeper somewhere, breathing. And toward evening, when the caravan stops at a wayside inn and the guards are lighting fires, he steps down from the wagon, stretches, and looks back the way they have come.

The road runs straight for a mile, white and empty, under a red sky.

Forty paces behind the last wagon, a man is standing in the road.

He is tall and thin and wears the plain gray of a Registry clerk, but without the plum seal, without the hat, without any badge at all. He stands with his hands loosely at his sides and his bare head tilted a little, like a man listening. He has no face that anyone could describe. It is not that it is hidden. It is that it will not stay in the memory; it slides away, like a name on the tongue.

Jian knows him. He knows him at once, from the Gate stair, from the day the envoy sat across a small table and offered him a seat.

The Nameless.

The figure inclines its head. Not in greeting. In acknowledgment, as one acknowledges a fellow traveler on a long road.

Then it sits down in the dust, crosses its legs, and begins, patiently, to wait.

Pebble has come up beside him. Her ears are flat.

"He has been following us since the gate," she says, in her clear low voice. "Forty paces. The whole day. He has not once closed the distance, and he has not once let it grow."
